title: Volunteer Code of Ethics
description: Understand the expectations that protect trust: serve sincerely, respect seniors and keep personal interests outside volunteering.
imageAlt: Seniors and younger people connecting through conversation

lesson.title: The expectations we bring to every interaction
lesson.introduction: Volunteering begins with a genuine heart to serve. These prototype expectations describe everyday conduct for volunteers and should be read alongside the centre's confirmed policies and staff guidance.

sections.heading: Serve without an external agenda
sections.body: Join because you care about seniors and want to contribute. Do not use volunteering to gain customers, leads, money, influence or private favours. An insurance agent must not sell or promote insurance to seniors, and a property agent must not market property or seek clients through volunteer relationships. This applies even if an opportunity seems convenient or the offer appears helpful.

sections.heading: Keep trust free from commercial pressure
sections.body: Do not circulate business cards, arrange private sales appointments, collect contact details for a business or refer seniors to your own paid services. A senior may feel obliged to agree because they trust you as a volunteer. If asked for commercial advice, explain your volunteer role and refer the request to centre staff rather than making a pitch.

sections.heading: Speak with respect and gentle words
sections.body: Use a calm voice, considerate language and good intentions. Address seniors as adults, listen fully and respect their preferences and choices. Do not mock, shame, threaten, argue aggressively or become hostile. If you feel frustrated, pause and ask a team member or staff member to support the interaction.

sections.heading: Learn with the whole team
sections.body: Each volunteer has something to learn from seniors, staff and other volunteers, regardless of age or experience. Ask questions, welcome feedback, share useful observations respectfully and give others space to contribute. Follow the agreed plan and ask for help instead of pretending to know.

sections.heading: Practise kindness, patience, generosity and honesty
sections.body: Kindness means noticing feelings and offering help with consent. Patience means allowing time without pressure. Generosity means sharing attention, effort and knowledge without expecting a return. Honesty means being truthful about your skills, mistakes and commitments; never promise support or outcomes you cannot provide.

sections.heading: Maintain boundaries and raise concerns
sections.body: Protect personal information and stay within the assigned volunteer role. Do not pursue private financial arrangements or use a senior's circumstances for personal benefit. Tell the supervising staff member promptly about a conflict of interest, inappropriate conduct or a mistake. Describe the facts calmly and let staff decide the next steps.

lesson.scenario: A senior asks whether you can help sell their flat after learning that you work in property. Say: 'I am here as a volunteer, so I cannot use this relationship for business. Let us ask the centre staff about an appropriate way to seek advice.' Do not exchange sales contacts or arrange a private appointment through the session.
takeaways: Bring a genuine heart to serve, with no sales or personal agenda.
Never market insurance, property or other paid services through volunteering.
Use gentle words; pause and seek support if an interaction becomes tense.
Learn from every team member and welcome feedback.
Show kindness, patience, generosity and honesty through actions.
Protect trust, keep appropriate boundaries and raise concerns with staff.

title: Kindness, Patience, Generosity and Honesty
description: Turn good intentions into practical behaviours when welcoming seniors, sharing tasks and working as a team.
imageAlt: Seniors joining community activities at an Active Ageing Centre

lesson.title: Values become visible in small actions
lesson.introduction: Upskilling is more than learning a task. It includes the habits that help another person feel respected, safe and able to participate. Practise one habit at each session, then reflect with your team.

sections.heading: Kindness: notice and ask
sections.body: Greet a quieter participant, learn their preferred name and ask what would make joining easier. Offer support without assuming they need it. A kind response preserves choice: 'Would you like some help, or would you prefer to try first?'

sections.heading: Patience: make room for another pace
sections.body: Allow time for an answer or a safe task. Avoid sighing, interrupting or rushing someone because the group is moving faster. Give one clear prompt, wait and check whether the person wants help. If you need a pause yourself, ask a teammate to step in calmly.

sections.heading: Generosity: give attention without a return
sections.body: Share your time, skills and encouragement without expecting praise, gifts, referrals or business. Invite another volunteer to learn alongside you, credit their contribution and leave space for seniors to teach you. Generosity does not mean making private financial commitments or stepping outside your role.

sections.heading: Honesty: be clear about what you can do
sections.body: Say 'I am not sure; let us ask the staff' when you do not know. Report mistakes promptly instead of hiding them, and tell the coordinator early if you cannot attend. Reliable, truthful communication helps the team plan and protects seniors from false expectations.

sections.heading: Reflect and grow together
sections.body: After a session, ask yourself: Who did I listen to? When did I feel impatient? What did another volunteer teach me? Choose one specific action to try next time. Discuss situations respectfully without sharing a senior's private details outside the authorised team.

lesson.scenario: A teammate explains an activity differently from you. Instead of criticising them in front of seniors, listen and support the shared task. Later, ask what worked for them, share your observation gently and agree with staff on any instructions that need to be consistent.
takeaways: Ask before helping and respect a person's answer.
Slow your response when frustration rises.
Give time and knowledge without seeking a personal return.
Be honest about uncertainty, mistakes and availability.
Treat every session as a chance to learn from the team.

title: Small Phrases, Stronger Connections
description: Practise simple greetings, ask about language preferences and learn unfamiliar dialect phrases with a fluent teammate.
imageAlt: Younger and older participants learning from one another during an activity

lesson.title: Start with a greeting, then listen
lesson.introduction: A few familiar words can make a welcome feel warmer. Ask which language or dialect the senior prefers; do not assume from appearance or name. The pronunciation guides below are approximate English cues, not a substitute for hearing a fluent speaker.

sections.heading: Ask for a preference
sections.body: Try: 'Which language would you feel most comfortable speaking?' Introduce yourself slowly and ask how the person likes to be addressed. If you do not share a language, use respectful gestures, simple words and an approved fluent teammate rather than speaking louder.

sections.heading: Mandarin: a respectful hello and thank you
sections.body: Hello: 您好 — nín hǎo (approximately 'neen how'). Thank you: 谢谢 — xièxie (approximately 'syeh-syeh'). Mandarin tones affect meaning; ask a fluent speaker to model each phrase and repeat it back before using it. Keep the exchange simple and be honest about how much Mandarin you understand.

sections.heading: Malay: good morning and thank you
sections.body: Good morning: Selamat pagi (approximately 'suh-lah-mat pah-gee'). Thank you: Terima kasih (approximately 'tuh-ree-mah kah-see'). Listen to the person's response and avoid continuing a memorised script if you do not understand. Ask a teammate to help the conversation continue.

sections.heading: Tamil: a greeting and thank you
sections.body: Hello: வணக்கம் — vaṇakkam (approximately 'va-nak-kam'). Thank you: நன்றி — naṉṟi, often written nandri (approximately 'nun-dree'). These English cues cannot represent every Tamil sound. Invite a fluent speaker to demonstrate, practise respectfully and welcome correction.

sections.heading: Learn dialects with people, not assumptions
sections.body: A senior may prefer Hokkien, Teochew, Cantonese or another variety, and words or pronunciation can differ between communities. Ask a fluent volunteer or staff member to teach a verified greeting used locally. Record the meaning and pronunciation only with permission; do not invent translations or assume all dialects are interchangeable.

sections.heading: Use language to connect, not to overclaim
sections.body: A greeting does not make you an interpreter. For consent, personal concerns, safety instructions or anything you cannot confidently understand, involve centre staff and appropriate language support. Do not guess a translation or put private information into a public translation service. Thank the senior for teaching you and keep learning with the team.

lesson.scenario: You greet a senior in Mandarin, but they answer in Hokkien and you cannot follow. Smile and explain: 'I am still learning. May I ask my teammate to help?' Find the approved fluent teammate, then learn one verified phrase together for the next visit.
takeaways: Ask about language and dialect preferences before assuming.
Start with a greeting and thanks, then practise with a fluent speaker.
Pronunciation cues are approximate; listen and welcome correction.
Do not pretend to understand or guess an important translation.
Seek staff and appropriate language support for sensitive or safety-related discussions.

title: Respectful Communication with Seniors
description: Practise listening, speaking clearly and creating conversations that protect dignity.
imageAlt: Seniors and younger people sharing a conversation

video.title: Watch: Conversations with seniors and children
video.introduction: Notice how curiosity, patience and shared stories help people of different ages connect naturally.

lesson.title: Make every conversation person-centred
lesson.introduction: Good communication begins with seeing the senior as a person with preferences, experience and agency—not as a task to complete.

sections.heading: Start with respect
sections.body: Introduce yourself, ask how the person prefers to be addressed and speak directly to them. Avoid childish language or assumptions based only on age.

sections.heading: Listen before solving
sections.body: Give the person time to finish. Use short follow-up questions and reflect back what you heard. A pause is not an invitation to answer on their behalf.

sections.heading: Make understanding easier
sections.body: Reduce background noise, face the person, speak clearly at a natural pace and check understanding without testing or embarrassing them.

lesson.scenario: Mr Lim pauses while telling a story and loses his train of thought. Stay relaxed, acknowledge what he has already shared and offer a gentle prompt rather than completing the story for him.
takeaways: Speak to the senior, not around them.
Use open questions and allow time for a response.
Check understanding respectfully instead of repeating more loudly.

quiz.question: A senior takes several seconds to answer. What should you do first?
options: Repeat the question more loudly
Wait calmly and maintain attentive body language
Ask someone else to answer
Change the subject immediately
quiz.feedback: Wait calmly and show that you are listening; the person may simply need time to think or find their words. Speaking louder assumes a hearing problem, answering through someone else removes their voice, and changing the subject can make their contribution feel unimportant.

quiz.question: Which opening is most respectful?
options: Hello auntie, I know what you need
Good morning, I’m Mei. How would you like me to address you?
Can your caregiver explain for you?
You probably cannot hear me, right?
quiz.feedback: Introduce yourself and ask the person's preference so they can shape the interaction from the start. Assuming their needs, bypassing them for a caregiver or making assumptions about hearing can undermine dignity before the conversation has begun.

quiz.question: How can you check understanding without sounding like a test?
options: Ask the person to repeat every word
Say the same sentence louder
Invite them to tell you what they would like to do next
Move on without checking
quiz.feedback: Invite the person to describe their preferred next step; this checks whether you share an understanding while keeping the exchange natural. Demanding a word-for-word answer may feel like a test, volume does not resolve every misunderstanding, and moving on can leave uncertainty unaddressed.

title: Choice, Dignity and Independence
description: Support seniors without taking over decisions or everyday tasks they can safely do.
imageAlt: A senior making an independent choice with support

video.title: Watch: Promoting choice and encouraging independence
video.introduction: Look for the difference between offering support and taking control away from someone.

lesson.title: Help with, not instead of
lesson.introduction: Volunteers can make activities more accessible while allowing each senior to decide, participate and contribute in their own way.

sections.heading: Offer real choices
sections.body: Present two or three suitable options in plain language. Give time to decide and accept the answer, including a decision not to participate.

sections.heading: Use the least help needed
sections.body: Ask before assisting. Begin with a verbal cue, then demonstrate, and only provide physical help when appropriate and consented to.

sections.heading: Protect capability
sections.body: Completing a task faster is not always better. Participation, confidence and independence may be the more important outcomes.

lesson.scenario: Mdm Tan is slowly arranging materials for a craft activity. Instead of taking over, ask whether she would like you to hold the tray, demonstrate one step or simply wait nearby.
takeaways: Ask permission before helping.
Offer manageable choices rather than making the decision.
Let the senior do every safe part they can manage.

quiz.question: A senior is completing a task slowly but safely. What is the best response?
options: Take over so the group can move faster
Let them continue and offer help if requested
Tell them to skip the activity
Ask another senior to finish it
quiz.feedback: Allow the senior to continue and offer help without taking control. Finishing for them or excluding them may save time, but it removes a chance to participate and can weaken confidence; speed alone is not the goal.

quiz.question: Which is a meaningful choice?
options: Do this activity now
Would you like painting or a word game?
Everyone else chose this, so you should too
You do not want to join, do you?
quiz.feedback: Offer a small number of clear, suitable options and accept the senior's decision. A command, peer pressure or a question that suggests the answer does not provide the same freedom to choose.

quiz.question: Before providing physical assistance, a volunteer should usually…
options: Act quickly without asking
Ask permission and follow staff guidance
Assume help is always welcome
Wait until the person becomes frustrated
quiz.feedback: Ask permission and follow the centre's guidance about the assistance you are authorised to provide. Acting on assumptions can startle the person or cross a boundary, while waiting for frustration misses the chance to offer respectful support early.

title: Dementia-Friendly Conversations
description: Respond to memory and communication changes with calm, clarity and connection.
imageAlt: A caregiver speaking calmly with an older adult

video.title: Watch: How Alzheimer’s affects communication
video.introduction: Focus on the communication barriers described and the practical ways a supporter can reduce pressure.

lesson.title: Connect instead of correcting
lesson.introduction: A person living with dementia may need more time, fewer distractions and simpler choices. Their feelings remain important even when details are confused.

sections.heading: Create the conditions
sections.body: Approach from the front, introduce yourself, make eye contact and reduce competing noise. One speaker and one idea at a time are easier to follow.

sections.heading: Use supportive language
sections.body: Keep sentences short, ask one question at a time and avoid arguing over a mistaken detail. Respond to the emotion and gently redirect when needed.

sections.heading: Notice non-verbal cues
sections.body: Facial expression, posture and behaviour can communicate discomfort, fatigue or anxiety. If something changes suddenly, inform centre staff.

lesson.scenario: A senior repeatedly asks when her mother will arrive. Do not challenge her with facts. Acknowledge that she misses her mother, offer reassurance and invite her into a familiar activity while informing staff if distress continues.
takeaways: Reduce distractions and communicate one idea at a time.
Validate feelings rather than arguing about facts.
Escalate sudden or concerning changes to centre staff.

quiz.question: A person living with dementia repeats the same question. What is most helpful?
options: Say that you already answered
Respond calmly and use a reassuring cue
Ignore every repeated question
Test whether they remember your name
quiz.feedback: Respond calmly and offer reassurance because a repeated question may reflect uncertainty or memory difficulty. Reminding the person that you already answered, ignoring them or testing memory can add embarrassment and pressure without meeting the concern behind the question.

quiz.question: Which environment best supports communication?
options: Several people speaking at once
Loud music and quick instructions
A quieter space with one speaker
Standing behind the person
quiz.feedback: Choose a quieter space and one speaker so the person has a clear voice and face to focus on. Competing voices, loud music, rushed instructions or speaking from behind add demands that can make understanding harder.

quiz.question: A senior becomes suddenly confused and unsteady. What should a volunteer do?
options: Diagnose the cause
Keep it secret
Inform centre staff promptly and stay within role
Postpone mentioning it until next week
quiz.feedback: Tell centre staff promptly what you observed and follow their directions within your volunteer role. Guessing a diagnosis exceeds that role, while secrecy or delay prevents staff from responding to a concerning change.

title: Falls Awareness and Safe Support
description: Spot common hazards, respond safely and know when to involve trained centre staff.
imageAlt: An older adult learning practical fall-prevention steps

video.title: Watch: Eight steps to help prevent a fall
video.introduction: Use the video as awareness training. Volunteers must follow NTUC Health procedures and staff instructions at all times.
video.source: Manitoba Health / Winnipeg Regional Health Authority

lesson.title: Notice, protect and escalate
lesson.introduction: Volunteers help by keeping shared spaces orderly, observing changes and contacting staff—not by performing clinical assessments or unsafe transfers.

sections.heading: Scan the environment
sections.body: Look for wet floors, trailing bags, unstable chairs, poor lighting and objects blocking walkways. Remove only simple hazards that are safe to handle and tell staff.

sections.heading: Support without pulling
sections.body: Do not lift, pull or physically transfer a senior unless you are trained, authorised and directed. Offer reassurance, create space and summon staff.

sections.heading: If a fall happens
sections.body: Stay with the person, call staff immediately and keep the area calm. Do not move them unless there is immediate danger and staff or emergency guidance directs it.

lesson.scenario: You notice Mr Rahman reaching for a chair that appears unstable. Ask him to pause, bring the concern to staff and clear nearby clutter. Do not grab or pull him unexpectedly.
takeaways: Keep walking routes clear and report hazards.
Never attempt an untrained lift or transfer.
After a fall, stay, call staff and avoid moving the person unnecessarily.

quiz.question: You see a loose bag strap across a walkway. What should you do?
options: Leave it for housekeeping
If safe, move it and inform staff
Wait for someone to trip
Cover it with paper
quiz.feedback: Remove the simple hazard only if you can do so safely, and tell staff so the walkway stays clear. Leaving it in place or waiting exposes others to a known obstacle; covering it with paper conceals the strap and can create another hazard.

quiz.question: A senior falls and says they are fine. What is the correct volunteer response?
options: Help them stand immediately
Leave to avoid embarrassment
Call centre staff and stay with them
Ask another senior to lift them
quiz.feedback: Call staff, stay with the senior and follow the centre's response procedure. Do not assume a reassuring comment rules out injury: an untrained lift can cause further harm, and leaving means the senior has no immediate support.

quiz.question: When may a volunteer perform a physical transfer?
options: Whenever the centre is busy
Only when trained, authorised and following procedure
Whenever the senior asks
After watching an online video
quiz.feedback: A physical transfer requires the relevant training, authorisation and the centre's procedure. A busy session, a request for help or an online video does not establish that you can assist safely; ask trained staff for support.

title: Digital Help Without Taking Over
description: Guide seniors through digital tasks while protecting passwords, money and personal information.
imageAlt: A senior learning how to identify an impersonation scam

video.title: Watch: Be Cyber Safe — impersonation scams
video.introduction: Look for warning signs and consider how to help a senior pause before acting on an urgent request.
video.source: Cyber Security Agency of Singapore / Digital for Life

lesson.title: Coach the steps; protect the person
lesson.introduction: Digital support should build confidence without exposing private information or letting the volunteer control accounts and transactions.

sections.heading: Let the senior stay in control
sections.body: Explain one step at a time and let the senior tap or type. Never ask them to say a password or one-time password aloud, and do not store credentials.

sections.heading: Pause urgent requests
sections.body: Scammers create urgency, secrecy and fear. Stop the interaction, do not click unfamiliar links and verify using an official number or website—not details supplied by the caller.

sections.heading: Escalate concerns
sections.body: Tell centre staff if a senior may be at risk. In Singapore, the ScamShield Helpline is 1799. For immediate danger or an active financial loss, follow staff and official emergency guidance.

lesson.scenario: A message claiming to be from a bank tells Mdm Lee to click immediately and enter an OTP. Ask her not to click, preserve the message, involve centre staff and verify through the bank’s official channel.
takeaways: Never handle passwords, OTPs or banking transactions.
Urgency and secrecy are common scam warning signs.
Verify independently and involve staff when concerned.

quiz.question: A senior asks you to type their bank password. What should you do?
options: Type it quickly
Ask them to tell you the password
Decline, protect their privacy and seek an approved support route
Photograph it for later
quiz.feedback: Decline respectfully and ask staff about an approved support route while the senior retains control of their account. Typing, hearing or photographing a password exposes private credentials and can place both the senior and volunteer at risk; helpful intentions do not remove that boundary.

quiz.question: Which is a strong scam warning sign?
options: A centre timetable
Pressure to act urgently and keep the request secret
A familiar family photo
A printed activity sheet
quiz.feedback: Pressure to act immediately and keep a request secret is a reason to pause and verify independently. These tactics discourage a person from checking with someone they trust; ordinary materials or a familiar image alone do not establish the same warning pattern.

quiz.question: How should a suspicious caller be verified?
options: Call the number they provide
Use an official website or known official number
Share the OTP to test them
Install the app they recommend
quiz.feedback: Find an official website or a known official number independently before taking further action. A number or app supplied by the caller may also be controlled by them, and sharing an OTP can expose an account rather than verify who is calling.

title: Bridging Generations Through Activities
description: Create inclusive interactions where younger and older participants learn from one another.
imageAlt: Younger and older people participating in an activity together

video.title: Watch: When seniors and juniors connect
video.introduction: Observe how shared activities can make conversation easier and allow every generation to contribute.

lesson.title: Design for mutual contribution
lesson.introduction: Intergenerational activities work best when seniors are collaborators with knowledge to share, not passive recipients of entertainment.

sections.heading: Begin with a shared task
sections.body: Games, music, simple crafts and storytelling give everyone something concrete to respond to and reduce the pressure of starting a conversation.

sections.heading: Balance participation
sections.body: Invite, do not force. Adapt pace, materials and instructions so that different abilities can contribute without singling anyone out.

sections.heading: Make experience visible
sections.body: Ask about memories, skills and preferences. Let seniors teach, demonstrate and make choices alongside younger participants.

lesson.scenario: During a music activity, invite seniors to suggest songs and share what they remember about them. Give children simple roles such as holding lyric cards or choosing the next prompt.
takeaways: Use an activity as a bridge, not a performance for seniors.
Adapt quietly so everyone can participate.
Create opportunities for seniors to lead and teach.

quiz.question: What best describes an inclusive intergenerational activity?
options: Young people perform while seniors only watch
Everyone has a suitable way to contribute
The fastest participant leads every task
All participants must do exactly the same thing
quiz.feedback: Offer meaningful roles that suit different abilities, interests and preferences. Requiring identical tasks or giving all leadership to the fastest person can exclude others, while treating seniors only as an audience misses opportunities for mutual contribution.

quiz.question: A senior declines an activity. What should the volunteer do?
options: Pressure them because participation is healthy
Accept the choice and offer another way to be included
Report them for being uncooperative
Remove them from the group
quiz.feedback: Accept the decision and offer another role, activity or the option to observe. Pressure, punishment or exclusion treats a personal preference as misbehaviour and can make the person less comfortable returning.

quiz.question: Which prompt supports mutual learning?
options: Let me show you the correct way
What games did you enjoy when you were younger?
This is too difficult for seniors
Please sit quietly while we finish
quiz.feedback: An open question about familiar games invites the senior to share knowledge and experience. Assuming you always know the correct way, describing tasks as too difficult for seniors or asking them to stay silent closes off their contribution.

title: Preparing for Centre and Home Visits
description: Arrive prepared, observe respectfully and follow boundaries during centre or outreach visits.
imageAlt: NTUC Health team members carrying out an Active Ageing Centre visit

video.title: Watch: NTUC Health Active Ageing Centres — smart home visits
video.introduction: Notice how visits are purposeful, coordinated and centred on the senior’s circumstances.

lesson.title: Prepare, observe and report
lesson.introduction: Every visit should follow the centre’s plan. Volunteers protect privacy, stay within the assigned role and report observations to staff.

sections.heading: Before the visit
sections.body: Attend the briefing, understand your role, know who is supervising and carry only approved materials. Do not make private arrangements outside the programme.

sections.heading: During the visit
sections.body: Introduce yourself and the purpose of the visit. Respect the home, do not photograph or share personal details, and avoid handling medication or money.

sections.heading: After the visit
sections.body: Report relevant observations factually to the assigned staff member. Do not diagnose, promise services or discuss the senior with people outside the authorised team.

lesson.scenario: During a visit, you notice unopened meals and that the senior seems unusually tired. Do not diagnose or promise help. Note what you observed and contact the supervising staff member promptly.
takeaways: Know your assigned role and supervisor before leaving.
Protect privacy and never share visit photos casually.
Report facts and concerns through the approved channel.

quiz.question: A senior asks you to buy medication using their bank card. What should you do?
options: Accept to be helpful
Decline and contact the supervising staff member
Ask for the PIN
Keep the card until next visit
quiz.feedback: Decline respectfully and bring the request to your supervising staff member so an appropriate arrangement can be considered. Taking the card, asking for a PIN or privately carrying out the errand crosses financial and role boundaries, even when the request is well intended.

quiz.question: What should a volunteer share after a concerning visit?
options: A diagnosis
Factual observations through the approved staff channel
A photo on social media
A promise that services will be arranged
quiz.feedback: Describe what you saw or heard through the approved staff channel, distinguishing observations from assumptions. A diagnosis exceeds the volunteer role, public photos expose privacy, and promises about services create expectations you may not be able to meet.

quiz.question: When is it acceptable to photograph a senior at home?
options: Whenever the photo is positive
Only under approved consent and programme procedures
When the senior is not looking
If the volunteer deletes it later
quiz.feedback: Use the organisation's approved consent and photography process before taking any photo. A positive image still involves privacy, unnoticed photography removes choice, and deleting an image later does not undo taking it without permission.

title: Creating Belonging at the AAC
description: Help each visitor feel noticed, included and connected to the life of the centre.
imageAlt: Seniors taking part in a welcoming Active Ageing Centre community

video.title: Watch: Living the kampung spirit at the Active Ageing Hub
video.introduction: Look for the everyday moments that turn a programme venue into a community where people know and support one another.

lesson.title: Turn attendance into connection
lesson.introduction: Belonging grows through consistent welcome, remembered preferences and opportunities to contribute—not only through large activities.

sections.heading: Welcome intentionally
sections.body: Greet people by their preferred name when known, explain what is happening and introduce newcomers to a staff member or activity buddy.

sections.heading: Notice the edges
sections.body: Look beyond the most vocal participants. Offer low-pressure ways to join, such as helping with materials, observing first or talking one-to-one.

sections.heading: Build continuity
sections.body: Remember appropriate preferences, follow up on previous conversations and help people connect with activities and peers that genuinely interest them.

lesson.scenario: A new visitor sits alone near the entrance. Introduce yourself, explain two activities taking place and offer to accompany them. Respect their choice if they prefer to observe first.
takeaways: A clear welcome reduces uncertainty.
Offer several levels of participation.
Small, consistent interactions create trust over time.

quiz.question: A newcomer prefers to watch an activity first. What should you do?
options: Insist that they join immediately
Welcome them, explain the activity and let them observe
Ignore them until they participate
Tell them the centre is only for active people
quiz.feedback: Offer a warm explanation and let the newcomer observe at their own pace. Insisting, ignoring them or suggesting they do not belong creates pressure; feeling welcome before joining can be an important first step.

quiz.question: Who may need extra attention in a lively group?
options: Only the loudest participants
People at the edges who have not found a way in
Only people who already know volunteers
Nobody if the activity is busy
quiz.feedback: Notice people at the edges and offer a gentle invitation with several ways to participate. Focusing only on loud or familiar participants can leave newcomers unseen, and a busy activity does not mean everyone feels included.

quiz.question: What builds trust most reliably?
options: One grand event
Consistent respectful interactions over time
Promising help outside your role
Knowing every personal detail
quiz.feedback: Reliable, respectful interactions and appropriate follow-up show that the senior can depend on you within your role. A single event cannot replace consistency, and overpromising or seeking unnecessary personal details can weaken the trust you want to build.
